name: Xokleng
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Gakran 2005 thesis and Gakran 2015 grammar both READ (PDFs online): zero mentions of acento/stress. Henry, Jules 1948. The Kaingang Language (IJAL 14) plausibly covers accent; JSTOR-only.

new_statements.quote: O acento lexical em Xokleng é previsível, ocorrendo na última sílaba. Por não apresentar um valor distintivo, não constitui um valor fonêmico e desta forma, sua representação a nível fonológico é dispensável. Entretanto, o acento nos poucos casos excepcionais de palavras paroxítonas será representado. Existem também alguns elementos átonos, pertencentes a classes de palavras fechadas, como pronomes, posposições e marcas aspectuais (184). (184) /ɔɡ/ ‘3.PL’ /ki/ ‘LOC’ /dẽ/ ‘ASP.EST’
new_statements.translation: Lexical stress in Xokleng is predictable, occurring on the last syllable. Since it has no distinctive value, it is not phonemic and so its representation at the phonological level is dispensable. However, stress in the few exceptional cases of paroxytone words will be represented. There are also some unstressed elements belonging to closed word classes, such as pronouns, postpositions and aspect markers (184). (184) /ɔɡ/ '3.PL' /ki/ 'LOC' /dẽ/ 'ASP.EST'
new_statements.citation: Jolkesky, Marcelo Pinho de Valhery (2010). Reconstrução fonológica e lexical do Proto-Jê Meridional. Dissertação de Mestrado, Instituto de Estudos da Linguagem, Universidade Estadual de Campinas. §4.4.3.2 'Rima' (within 4.4.3 'Padrão silábico e acentual', Xokleng chapter), p. 115.
new_statements.locator: p. 115 (PDF page 143), §4.4.3.2, paragraph after the syllable-count table; example (184)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable of the (phonological) word; it is predictable and non-contrastive. Phonetic transcriptions in the same chapter show final stress in disyllables, e.g. /dɛbɤɡ/ [n̪d̪ɛˈmbəɡŋ] 'timbó', /kɔɟɡɤɡ/ [kɔj.ˈŋɡəɡŋ] 'homem' (p. 114).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Xokleng; the thesis's symbol list defines ˌ as 'acento de proeminência secundário' (p. xxi-ish, line 613 of text layer) but no secondary-stress marks or rules appear in the Xokleng section.
new_statements.exceptions: 'a few exceptional cases of paroxytone words' (to be marked in representation, none listed on p. 115); closed-class unstressed elements: pronouns, postpositions, aspect markers, e.g. /ɔɡ/ 3PL, /ki/ LOC, /dẽ/ stative aspect.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word-level stress ('acento lexical'); simple words are up to four syllables, mostly mono- and disyllabic (p. 115). The author's Xokleng data combine his own fieldwork at T.I. Ibirama (2009-2010, ~450 items) with Henry 1935/1948, Bridgeman 1958 and Wiesemann 1958 wordlists, Bublitz 1994, Oliveira et al. 2003 and Gakran's 2010 minidictionary (p. 19). Same final-stress statement is made for Kaingang (p. 78, >99% of words) and reconstructed for Proto-Southern Jê (p. 213).
new_statements.identity_note: Jolkesky 2010 describes Xokleng = Laklãnõ of T.I. Ibirama (Vale do Itajaí, SC), the single surviving community; this is xokl1240 itself, no dialect split. Henry 1935/1948 call the same Duque de Caxias (Dalbergia/Ibirama) community 'Kaingang'; his data are Xokleng, not Kaingang (kain1272).

sources.citation: Henry, Jules (1948). The Kaingang Language. International Journal of American Linguistics 14(3): 194-204. DOI 10.1086/464002. (Xokleng of the Duque de Caxias post, Dalbergia/Ibirama, SC.)
sources.note: Sections 1-3 (consonants, vowels, phonetic changes, pp. 194-196) give no stress-placement statement; stress appears only inside rules: 'm, n, and ñ may be converted into nasally exploded plosives when they occur immediately after an accented syllable' (p. 196) and fn. 19 'the glottal plosive appears between an accented vowel and the one that precedes it'. Word patterns: ~90% of words mono- or bisyllabic (p. 196).

sources.note: No placement statement; only 'in unaccented position' (affricate allophony, p. 174) and 'immediately after an accented syllable' (nasal plosive rule).
